topic: Groin pain in soccer and footy players

slides.headline: Groin grumbling after footy or soccer?
slides.sub: Kicking, sprinting and quick turns load the groin heaps. Here's what helps.

slides.title: Why kicking sports load the groin
slides.body: Kicking, cutting and sprinting ask the inner thigh and lower tummy muscles to work hard at long lengths. Groin pain often builds when training load jumps faster than those muscles can adapt.

slides.title: Strength beats rest on its own
slides.body: Rest may settle things, but the pain often returns with the next big game. Research suggests progressive adductor strengthening, like side-lying squeezes and Copenhagen planks, can help most players get back.

slides.title: Watch the weekly load
slides.body: Sudden jumps in training, back-to-back games or a switch to harder pitches are common triggers. Keep changes gradual and note how your groin feels the morning after each session.

slides.title: Warm up with purpose
slides.body: Before training, add side lunges, leg swings and a few gentle ball squeezes. Build up to sharp changes of direction rather than going straight into full-pace kicking drills.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: Pain that builds rather than settles, pain with coughing or sneezing, a lump in the groin, or hip pain at night is worth an assessment. Sudden sharp pain with bruising needs prompt attention.

slides.body: Our Chatswood and Sydney CBD physios assess your hip, groin and training load, then build a strength plan around your games. Book online, link in bio.

topic: Pilates for men: more than stretching

slides.headline: Think Pilates is just stretching?
slides.sub: Clinical Pilates is strength training on springs. Plenty of blokes find it humbling.

slides.title: It's resistance training, just quieter
slides.body: Reformer springs add load in both directions, so muscles work while lengthening and shortening. You can train legs, trunk and shoulders with real resistance, minus the clanging plates.

slides.title: Control is the hard part
slides.body: Moving slowly through full range is often harder than it looks. Plenty of strong gym-goers are surprised how much a controlled single-leg press or side plank variation asks of them.

slides.title: It fills gaps the gym misses
slides.body: Heavy lifting often skips rotation, single-leg control and strength at end range. Pilates can build those qualities, which carry over to running, golf, footy and lifting itself.

slides.title: A good fit around niggles
slides.body: If your back, hip or shoulder is grumbling, springs let you keep training while the load is adjusted. Clinical Pilates is guided by an assessment, so the program suits your body.

slides.title: You don't need to be flexible
slides.body: Tight hamstrings and a stiff back are reasons to start, not reasons to stay away. Flexibility usually improves as a side effect of moving through more range with control.

topic: Sports massage vs remedial massage: what's the difference?

slides.title: Remedial massage: assessment first

slides.title: Sports massage: built around training
slides.body: Sports massage is usually shaped by your training cycle. It may be brisker before an event and slower during a recovery week, focusing on the muscles your sport loads most.

slides.title: The overlap is big
slides.body: Many techniques are the same: soft tissue work, trigger point pressure and stretching. The real difference is the reason for the session, so tell your therapist what you want from it.

slides.title: A quick way to choose
slides.body: Got a specific niggle, like a sore neck or tight hip? Remedial is a good starting point. Deep in a training block with heavy legs? A sports-focused session may suit better.

slides.title: Keep expectations realistic
slides.body: Massage can help you feel looser and recover more comfortably. It works well alongside strength, sleep and sensible load, rather than replacing rehab when something keeps coming back.

topic: How to describe your pain at your first appointment

slides.headline: Hard to explain your pain? Try this
slides.sub: Five details that help your practitioner understand what's going on.

slides.title: Where it is, and where it spreads
slides.body: Point to the spot and trace where it travels, if it does. Pain that stays in one area and pain that runs down an arm or leg can point to different things.

slides.title: What it feels like
slides.body: Words like dull, sharp, burning, aching, throbbing or tingling all give useful clues. There's no wrong answer, so use your own words, even if they sound a bit odd.

slides.title: What makes it better or worse
slides.body: Notice what eases it and what stirs it up. Morning versus evening, sitting versus walking, and how it behaves after exercise all help shape your plan.

slides.title: How it started and changed
slides.body: Was there a clear moment, like a lift or a fall, or did it creep in? Is it improving, steady or building? A quick timeline in your phone makes this easy.

slides.title: What you want to get back to
slides.body: Tell us what matters most, whether that's sleeping through, lifting your kids or finishing a 10km run. Goals help your practitioner choose what to work on first.

slides.headline: Jot it down before you come

topic: Questions worth asking your practitioner

slides.headline: Five questions to ask your practitioner
slides.sub: Good questions make your plan clearer and easier to stick to.

slides.title: What do you think is going on?
slides.body: Ask for a plain-English explanation of what's likely driving your symptoms. If a term sounds like jargon, ask what it means. Understanding the why makes the exercises make sense.

slides.title: What should I do, and avoid?
slides.body: Ask which activities are fine to keep doing and which to ease back on for now. Most people can stay more active than they expect with a few sensible changes.

slides.title: How will we measure progress?
slides.body: Ask what markers you'll track, like walking distance, sleep, strength or a specific movement. Clear markers make progress easier to see, even when pain goes up and down.

slides.title: What's a realistic timeframe?
slides.body: Every body is different, but your practitioner can usually give a rough guide and explain what might speed things up or slow them down. Ask when you'll review the plan together.

slides.title: What if it flares up?
slides.body: Flare-ups are common and usually settle. Ask what to do if symptoms spike, which exercises to scale back, and when it's worth getting in touch rather than waiting.

topic: Getting the most from your appointment time

topic: Surfing: shoulder and neck care for paddling

slides.headline: Paddle-tired shoulders this surf season?
slides.sub: Paddling is most of surfing. Here's how to keep shoulders and neck happy.

slides.title: Paddling is the main event
slides.body: Most of a surf session is spent paddling, not riding waves. That's hundreds of shoulder strokes with your neck extended to look ahead, so both areas need capacity.

slides.title: Ease into the season
slides.body: If you've been out of the water over winter, start with shorter sessions and build over a few weeks. Shoulders adapt well when the load increases gradually.

slides.title: Strengthen the back of the shoulder
slides.body: Band external rotations, rows and prone Y raises build the muscles that control the shoulder blade. Two or three sessions a week on land can make paddling feel easier.

slides.title: Give your neck a breather
slides.body: Holding your head up while paddling loads the neck. Rest your chin briefly between sets, and try chin nods and mid-back extension over a rolled towel at home.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: Pain that wakes you at night, weakness lifting the arm, a shoulder that feels loose or pops out, or neck pain spreading down the arm with pins and needles is worth an assessment.

topic: Sleeping in a different bed on holiday

slides.headline: Holiday bed, not-so-holiday back
slides.sub: Why a different mattress can leave you stiff, and what helps.

slides.title: New surfaces take adjusting to
slides.body: A firmer or softer mattress and unfamiliar pillows change how your neck and back are supported. Stiffness for the first night or two is common and usually eases once you're moving.

slides.title: Pack your own pillow
slides.body: If your neck is fussy, bring the pillow you already sleep well on. A rolled towel to adjust the height of a hotel pillow is a handy backup if luggage space is tight.

slides.title: Tweak the setup you've got
slides.body: Bed too soft? A pillow under or between your knees can make lying more comfortable. Too firm? A folded blanket under your hips and shoulders can ease the pressure points.

slides.title: Move before you judge the day
slides.body: Morning stiffness often loosens with gentle movement. A short walk, knee rocks and a few slow neck turns before breakfast usually help more than lying in longer.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: Pain that keeps worsening, spreads down an arm or leg with numbness, or comes with fever or feeling unwell is worth checking with a health professional rather than waiting it out.

topic: Soft sand running: build up gradually

slides.headline: Soft sand is a different sport
slides.sub: Beach runs load your calves and Achilles far more than the footpath.

slides.title: Why sand feels so much harder
slides.body: Your foot sinks and slides with every step, so calves, Achilles and feet work harder to push off. Your pace drops, but the effort and the load climb.

slides.title: Start short, then build
slides.body: Begin with five to ten minutes of soft sand within your usual run, then add a few minutes each week. Firm sand near the water is a gentler stepping stone.

slides.title: Barefoot or shoes?
slides.body: Both are fine, but barefoot adds more load to the feet and calves. If you're new to sand, start in shoes or keep barefoot sections short and build from there.

slides.title: Watch the slope
slides.body: Beaches often slope towards the water, which tilts your hips and loads one side more. Run out and back so each leg gets the high side, or stick to flatter stretches.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: Achilles or calf pain that builds during runs, morning stiffness that lingers, a sudden pop at the back of the leg, or pain that changes how you walk deserves an assessment.

topic: Pilates and scoliosis: what to expect

slides.headline: Scoliosis and Pilates: what to expect
slides.sub: Realistic goals, sensible exercise and how a program is shaped.

slides.title: Scoliosis is common and varied
slides.body: Scoliosis means the spine has a sideways curve, often with some rotation. Many people live active, comfortable lives with it, and curves vary a lot from person to person.

slides.title: Set realistic goals
slides.body: Pilates isn't about straightening the spine or chasing a perfect posture. Goals usually centre on strength, control, comfort and confidence in movement, so everyday tasks and exercise feel easier.

slides.title: It starts with an assessment
slides.body: Your physio or instructor looks at how you move, breathe and load each side of your body. Exercises are then chosen to suit your curve, your symptoms and the activities you want to do.

slides.title: Both sides still get trained
slides.body: It's common to feel differences side to side. Programs often include some side-specific work, but general strength and mobility on both sides remain the foundation of most sessions.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: A curve that seems to be changing, new or worsening pain, numbness or weakness in the legs, or changes to your breathing are all worth discussing with your GP or specialist.

topic: Exercising in the heat: staying safe this summer

slides.headline: Training in the heat? Adjust the plan
slides.sub: Simple ways to keep exercising safely through a hot Sydney summer.

slides.title: Shift the clock
slides.body: Early morning or evening sessions are usually cooler. On very hot days, swap a hard outdoor session for an easier one, or move it somewhere air-conditioned.

slides.title: Slow down on purpose
slides.body: Heart rate climbs faster in the heat, so the same pace feels harder. Run or ride by effort rather than pace, and expect your times to drop for a while.

slides.title: Acclimatise over a couple of weeks
slides.body: Your body usually adapts to heat over roughly one to two weeks of regular, shorter sessions. Build duration gradually rather than starting with your longest effort.

slides.title: Drink before you're parched
slides.body: Start sessions well hydrated and sip regularly on longer efforts. For long, very sweaty sessions, electrolytes can help. Light, loose clothing and a hat help too.

slides.title: When to stop and get help
slides.body: Stop if you feel dizzy, nauseous or confused, stop sweating, or get a headache that keeps building. Cool down in the shade. Confusion or collapse is an emergency, so call 000.

topic: Tight hamstrings: massage, stretching and strength

slides.headline: Hamstrings always tight? Try all three
slides.sub: Massage, stretching and strength each play a different role.

slides.title: Tight doesn't always mean short
slides.body: Hamstrings can feel tight because they're tired, protective or underloaded, not only because they lack length. That's why stretching alone doesn't always change the feeling for long.

slides.title: Where massage fits
slides.body: Remedial massage can help tight hamstrings feel easier and make movement more comfortable in the short term. It's a useful window to follow up with movement and strength work.

slides.title: Stretch, but keep it easy
slides.body: Gentle, regular stretching, like a supported hamstring stretch held for about 30 seconds, can improve how much stretch you tolerate. It shouldn't feel sharp or nervy.

slides.title: Strength is the long game
slides.body: Bridges, Romanian deadlifts and slow hamstring curls build capacity through range. Two sessions a week is a good starting point, and many people find their hamstrings feel less tight once they're stronger.

slides.title: Check the back and nerves too
slides.body: Tightness with tingling, pain down the leg or low back pain may involve more than muscle, such as the lower back or a nerve. Your therapist may suggest a physio or GP assessment if so.

topic: Neck pain from scrolling your phone in bed

slides.headline: Scrolling in bed, stiff neck by morning?
slides.sub: Phone habits at night can load your neck. Small changes help.

slides.title: It's the long hold, not the phone
slides.body: Lying propped on a pillow with your chin tucked towards a screen holds your neck in one position for ages. Necks tolerate most positions, just not hours of the same one.

slides.title: Bring the phone up to you
slides.body: Lie on your side with the phone at eye level, or sit up with a pillow behind your back. Keeping your head closer to neutral eases the load on your neck.

slides.title: Set a scroll limit
slides.body: A timer or app limit helps you notice how long you've been in one position. Changing position every ten minutes or so is usually enough to take the edge off.

slides.title: Loosen up in the morning
slides.body: Gentle chin nods, slow head turns and shoulder rolls before you get out of bed can ease morning stiffness. Most neck stiffness settles within a few days with movement.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: Neck pain with pins and needles or weakness in the arm, severe headaches, dizziness, or pain that keeps building instead of settling is worth an assessment.

topic: Working overhead: painting, hanging lights and your neck

slides.headline: Painting the ceiling? Spare your neck
slides.sub: Overhead jobs can leave your neck and shoulders sore. Try this.

slides.title: Why overhead jobs feel rough
slides.body: Looking up for long periods holds the neck tipped back while your shoulders work above head height. It's the combination and the time, not the task itself, that tends to cause soreness.

slides.title: Get closer to the job
slides.body: Use a stable ladder or platform so the work sits closer to eye level. The less you tip your head back, the longer your neck can comfortably keep going.

slides.title: Work in short blocks
slides.body: Try 10 to 15 minutes overhead, then a short break looking down or straight ahead. Switch hands on the roller or drill where you can to share the load.

slides.title: Loosen up afterwards
slides.body: Gentle chin nods, shoulder rolls and a slow walk after the job help your neck recover. Most soreness from a big day settles within a few days with movement.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: Pain spreading down the arm, pins and needles, dizziness when looking up, or headaches that keep building are worth an assessment. Any fall from a ladder should be checked promptly.

slides.body: Our Chatswood and Sydney CBD physios assess your neck and shoulders, then give you simple exercises for the jobs ahead. Book online, link in bio.

slides.body: Next comes a look at how you move. Expect range of motion, strength and specific tests, all explained as you go. You can pause or ask questions at any point.

slides.body: Your physio gives a plain-English explanation of what's likely contributing to your symptoms, and whether anything needs a referral back to your GP or for imaging.

slides.body: Most first sessions include some treatment, which may be hands-on work, exercise, advice on daily activities, or a mix. It's tailored to you and what you're comfortable with.

topic: Tight chest and rounded shoulders: where massage fits

slides.headline: Tight chest, rounded shoulders?
slides.sub: Where remedial massage fits, and what else helps your shoulders sit easier.

slides.title: Why the chest gets tight
slides.body: Long hours at a desk, driving and phone use keep your arms forward. The chest muscles get used to that position and can feel tight when you reach overhead or open your arms wide.

slides.title: What massage can do
slides.body: Remedial massage to the chest, front of the shoulder and upper back can help these areas feel easier and make opening out more comfortable. It's most useful paired with movement.

slides.title: Open up in a doorway
slides.body: A doorway chest stretch, with forearms on the frame and a gentle step forward, held for about 30 seconds, is a simple option to repeat a few times through the day.

slides.title: Strengthen the back half
slides.body: Rows, band pull-aparts and face pulls train the muscles behind the shoulder. Most people find their shoulders sit more comfortably when the back is as strong as the front.

slides.title: Chest pain is different
slides.body: Muscle tightness usually changes with movement or touch. Chest pain with shortness of breath, sweating, nausea or pain spreading to the jaw or arm needs urgent medical help. Call 000.

topic: Corked thigh: what helps in the first few days

slides.headline: Corked thigh: go gentle early on
slides.sub: What tends to help in the days after a knock to the thigh.

slides.title: What a cork actually is
slides.body: A corked thigh is a deep bruise in the thigh muscle, usually from a knee or hard knock in contact sport. Bleeding in the muscle causes pain, swelling and stiffness.

slides.title: First 48 hours: calm it down
slides.body: Relative rest, ice for about 15 to 20 minutes every couple of hours, compression and elevation are common early steps. Resting with the knee gently bent can help too.

slides.title: Skip the HARM early on
slides.body: In the first couple of days, avoid heat, alcohol, running and massage on the area. These can increase bleeding in the muscle and may slow early recovery.

slides.title: Get moving gradually
slides.body: As pain allows, gentle knee bending, walking and light cycling help restore movement. Build towards jogging and sport in steps rather than testing it with a flat-out sprint.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: Swelling or pain that keeps increasing, a thigh that feels very tight or numb, being unable to bend the knee, or a lump that stays hard deserves prompt medical assessment.

topic: Pilates through menopause: strength and confidence

slides.headline: Menopause: a great time to get stronger
slides.sub: Where clinical Pilates fits for strength, bones and confidence in midlife.

slides.title: Muscle and bone need load
slides.body: Hormone changes around menopause are linked to faster loss of muscle and bone. Research suggests regular, progressive resistance exercise is one of the most helpful ways to support both.

slides.title: Springs make load adjustable
slides.body: Reformer springs let you add resistance gradually, so you can build strength at your own pace. Exercises can progress as you get stronger or be eased back on tougher days.

slides.title: Achy joints can still move
slides.body: Many people notice more joint aches through this stage. Controlled movement through a comfortable range often helps joints feel less stiff, and your program can work around sore spots.

slides.title: Pelvic floor is part of it
slides.body: Pelvic floor changes are common in midlife. Pilates can include pelvic floor awareness alongside the bigger muscle groups, and it's always fine to raise questions about it.

slides.title: Confidence counts too
slides.body: Feeling strong and steady on your feet can make everyday tasks, travel and sport feel more doable. Many people find regular sessions become a routine they genuinely look forward to.

topic: Lower back pain when standing still

slides.headline: Standing still is harder than walking
slides.sub: Why queues and events make your lower back ache, and what helps.

slides.title: Why standing still grumbles
slides.body: Standing in one spot keeps the same muscles and joints loaded without a break. Many people find walking feels fine, but queues, events or cooking tire the lower back quickly.

slides.title: Shift your weight often
slides.body: Move from one foot to the other, rock gently forward and back, or take a few steps whenever you can. Small, regular movements share the load around your back and hips.

slides.title: Use a step or ledge
slides.body: Resting one foot on a low step, rail or ledge changes the position of your pelvis and lower back. Swap feet every few minutes, whether you're at a bench or in the kitchen.

slides.title: Build standing endurance
slides.body: Glute bridges, side planks and hip hinges strengthen the muscles that support you when standing. A few sessions a week can make long stretches on your feet more comfortable.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: Leg pain, numbness or heaviness that comes on with standing or walking and eases with sitting, or back pain that keeps worsening, is worth an assessment.
